articles.title: Premature review – sunny charm provides screwball energy for surprise-pregnancy comedy
articles.summary: First-time director Kevin Walls creates a film sweet-natured enough to cancel out some comedy misfires as flatmates Eilidh and Cameron prepare for parenthood. The pram in the hallway is the enemy of good art, or so the famous quote goes.
body: Elle Watson is artist Eilidh, who works as a barista in a museum cafe. She has a friends-with-benefits setup with her flatmate Cameron (James Rottger); he has a job in finance and, after two degrees, a mountain of student debt and years in a mind-numbing entry-level position, he’s finally lined up an interview for his dream job. It would be crazy to have the baby, but Eilidh doesn’t take the abortion tablets. She can’t give Cameron a coherent reason why not; fair enough, it’s her decision, a gut feeling. Walls sensibly doesn’t go anywhere near the pro-choice/anti-abortion debate.

But it is a shame his script seems to naturally click more with Cameron’s point of view as he agonises about how a baby will impact his career. Eilidh cheerfully breezes through pregnancy – though inexplicably she turns mumzilla in one scene, demanding that Cameron help her break into a house to steal a secondhand cot, wearing tights over their heads. It’s a scene that reduces the film’s IQ and likability by about 10%. Elsewhere, there are some moments of gentleness, like Cameron’s lovely dad and his no-nonsense wisdom. “Life doesn’t give two shits about your plans, son.”
points: First-time director Kevin Walls creates a film sweet-natured enough to cancel out some comedy misfires as flatmates Eilidh and Cameron prepare for parenthood.

articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the rat who jumped off the wardrobe and flew at my face
articles.summary: There was a rat army in my flatshare, gnawing through pipes, carpets and even a bedroom door. That’s not to mention the mice... We should have known we were in trouble when we saw that the garden of our new place backed on to a Chinese restaurant in Hackney, London, with terrible reviews.
body: There was no stopping them. After sniffing out the remnants of an old snack in my housemate Simon’s bin, a pack of rats got to work one night gnawing through the wood at the bottom of his bedroom door. Like a rodent military exercise, they spent eight hours whittling a hole large enough to get through. I lay next door, 100% freaked out, panicking they’d try to get into my room next. I didn’t sleep a wink. Fairly soon after this, one of the rats died under the floorboards so we got a bottle-fly infestation to boot. Naturally, our landlord did nothing about any of this.

We tried not to kill them – in fact, Simon the pacifist locked a bunch in the saucepan cupboard using a wooden spoon. One day, he and I trapped one in his bedroom with us. It tried to get away from us by climbing to the top of the wardrobe. Suddenly, it jumped, body splayed, and flew at my face, ran down the entire length of my body and scuttled over my feet. Jonathan, our other housemate, walloped my toes with the metal pole, mistaking me for the rat.

articles.title: Solo autumn walks for women in the UK and Europe: ‘it should be fun, not daunting’
articles.summary: Hiking alone in the countryside can be joyous, but for women it can sometimes feel unnerving. Here’s how to enjoy it safely, plus four stunning routes to walk solo. I did my first solo hike during a sunny September, seven years ago.
body: But I was nervous. Not of being on my own, but of what might happen to me with no one around to help (breaking a bone, encountering a psychopath, being chased by a bull, getting fatally lost). I could have found a companion or joined a group, but my need for silence and solitude outweighed my fears.

It seems that many women feel the same: in the UK, the proportion of women solo hiking surged by 27% between 2020 and 2022. In America, 41 % of female hikers report regularly walking alone. And yet many women, although keen to do something similar, feel intimidated. According to researchers at the Munich University of Applied Sciences who are studying solo female walkers, 30% of women interviewed said they would like to hike solo but are hesitant.

In truth, women have long enjoyed a tradition of solo walking. From religious pilgrims to goat herders to 19th-century adventurers, there have always been women wandering, radically alone, through wild landscapes. But for those new to it, I’d say the best way to overcome your fear is to do it – and I’ve learned some simple ways to make the experience fun, not daunting.

articles.title: The pirates arrived with AK-47s. They took us hostage – then the torture began
articles.summary: Chirag Bahri was working on board a tanker when six men seized it. For almost eight months, he and his colleagues were held captive, an experience that would change his life for ever. It was at noon on 8 May 2010 when the pirates came.
body: The ship had been 120 miles off the coast of Oman, partway through a run taking benzene – a raw material used in petrochemicals – from Kandla Port in India to Antwerp in Belgium. The piracy problem in the Indian Ocean was well known; Somalis armed with AK-47s were setting out in fast skiffs and taking ships hostage. Yet commercial vessels, including the Marida Marguerite, remained undefended.

Big ships are slow and small skiffs are fast. The Marguerite was doing 13 knots; the pirates could do 25 – and they knew to approach in the shadow cast by the funnel on the water, so they were invisible until the last minute. There was nothing the crew could do to defend the ship anyway. All they had was razor wire and luck.

When Bahri arrived at the bridge, the pirates, carrying AK-47s, shouted at him to sit down. “I was terrified. I thought, my God, this is the end.” The crew were sitting on the floor. Several were crying; others were comforting their crewmates, saying, “No, they won’t kill us. This is business.”

articles.title: Céline Dion’s Paris Comeback Finds Fabulousness in the Fragile
articles.summary: Paris is alight with Céline Dion fever, and the first night of her five-week residency marked a powerful new chapter in the performer’s legendary career.
body: “ L’histoire! L’histoire! ” a family of at least three generations of Céline Dion fans shout as they pose for a camera, sporting at least double the number of merch styles. It’s the first night of the Canadian star’s 26-night residency in Paris after six years away from the stage, and the sense of occasion is significant, to put it mildly.

In 2022, Dion was diagnosed with stiff-person syndrome, a rare, debilitating progressive neurological disorder that causes muscle rigidity and spasms so violent Dion broke ribs. Her pain—and the possibility that she would never perform again—was captured in the vulnerable 2024 documentary I Am Céline Dion. Her electrifying performances, that legendarily belted F5 on “All By Myself,” her powerful yet playful command of the stage, an archive of stage-sweeping gowns… all of that might have been banished to memory. So when, in late March, Dion announced her Paris dates, her legions of fans were prepared to meet the moment.

articles.title: Beyoncé’s Cécred Is Entering Its Next Chapter
articles.summary: Beyoncé's Cécred is launching in UK retailer Space NK, as the two-year-old brand continues to grow, based on a strong consumer community. Vogue Business sat down with vice chairwoman Tina Knowles and CEO Grace Ray, to chart the brand’s path.
body: When I ask Ms. Tina Knowles, vice chairwoman of her daughter Beyoncé Knowles-Carter’s haircare label Cécred, how the brand has performed since its launch, she paints me a picture.

“I’m in airports probably twice a week, and without fail, there are people in the airport or on the flight showing me the results of Cécred,” she says, speaking on Zoom. Often, they even ask her to touch and see how great their hair feels. “My kids tell me all the time, ‘Mom, you can’t be putting your hands in people’s hair,’” she laughs. “But people want to show me their results — I can’t help it. The response has been overwhelming.”

Beyoncé launched Cécred — a science-backed haircare label focused on hair and scalp health — in February 2024, alongside her mom and brand CEO and beauty veteran Grace Ray (who previously led prestige haircare brand Living Proof, and held roles at Smashbox and L’Oréal). Designed to improve the health and condition of all types of hair, the team spent six years before launch researching and developing patent-pending formulas that claim to improve hair and scalp health for all types and textures.
points: Beyoncé's Cécred is launching in UK retailer Space NK, as the two-year-old brand continues to grow, based on a strong consumer community.

articles.title: Serpentine’s Hans Ulrich Obrist: Creatives Must Help Shape AI
articles.summary: As Serpentine launches a new R&D fellowship exploring AI’s impact on cultural production, its artistic director argues creatives must be given a say in the tech that will transform their industries.
body: As generative AI has become better at producing convincing — if not hyper-polished — images, video and other creative work in the past year, the debate around its role in culture is moving beyond whether artists should use it. More pressing questions are emerging around authorship, ownership and creative control — and whether artists can help shape the technology itself, rather than simply respond to it.

The Serpentine has been commissioning artists and developing research around emerging technology since it launched its Arts Technologies program in 2014, but this is the first fellowship the gallery has launched dedicated to R&D in the area.

“The fellowship is founded on the belief that artists are not simply observers of technological change, but essential contributors to it, creating opportunities for practitioners to shape wider conversations about how emerging technologies are governed,” the Serpentine Gallery said, adding that the artists were selected for their approach to the tech “not as a finished product, but as an unsettled terrain whose assumptions, limits and possibilities need to be redrawn.”

articles.title: I Spent Four Days Touring Scotland’s Whisky Island—and It Was Better Than I Expected
articles.summary: One writer's experience taking a small-group tour of Islay with her dad, visiting historic distilleries, sampling smoky drams, and discovering why the island is worth the journey.
body: My dad’s 60th birthday was coming up, and as an avid whisky drinker with a particularly sharp nose, his dream trip has always been to explore the coastline of Islay, a Scottish island famed worldwide for its smoky, peated single malt whiskies. I often travel solo and am fond of organized tours, so when I came across Rabbie’s four-day Islay and whisky tour —with pickup from Edinburgh, a selection of historic stops, a maximum group size of 16 people, and plenty of opportunities for drams—it sounded ideal for us both.

Islay is the southernmost island of the Inner Hebrides, with a landscape of rugged beaches and peat bogs, and traveling through it usually involves many small logistics. I was thrilled to see that this tour handles all of the planning for you—including transportation, accommodations, attractions, and providing a local guide for the four-day trip. It starts at just $609 per adult without accommodations or distillery tours, or around $1,464 all-in, which seemed like a great deal. I was convinced, so I booked it!

articles.title: The Case for Taking Kids on Big Trips—Even Those That Sound Like a Terrible Idea
articles.summary: One writer counts safaris, Mardi Gras, and an India excursion among her mother-toddler trips. Here's why she has rarely, if ever, regretted it.
body: I have a long track record of making ill-advised—occasionally unhinged—family-travel decisions. My son Julian’s first interstate trip was to Wisconsin to go ice fishing at five weeks old. At 20 months, I took him—just the two of us—on a 23-day trip through Oman, Tanzania, and the United Arab Emirates to road trip across the Wahiba Sands and Hajar Mountains before flying off on safari. Friends thought I’d lost it. My husband wished me luck and stayed home.

A year later, Julian and I left for 88 days and 14 countries across six continents. Our stint in India, which set off alarm bells with family, was one of my favorite stops: In the glorious sensory overload of Varanasi and Delhi, Julian’s loudness barely registered; I could finally exhale.

I waited a long time to have a child because I wasn’t sure I wanted one—or was particularly cut out to be somebody’s mom. Parenthood has changed how I assess risk, but fear has never gotten much of a vote in my life, and I don’t want it calling the shots in his either. Sometimes the whole thing blows up in your face. But I’ve learned not to confuse a hard trip with a bad one.

articles.title: How to Boil Potatoes (and How Long to Boil Them)
articles.summary: Two keys to perfectly boiled potatoes: time and salt. (Like, a lot of salt.)
body: So many potato recipes start with the same instruction: “Boil the potatoes.” Simple enough—until you’re wondering whether to start them in cold or boiling water, how much salt to add, or how long the potatoes actually need to cook.

The short version: Start potatoes in cold, well-salted water, bring it to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer until tender. That’s it! Depending on their size and what you’re making, the actual cooking time could range from 8–40 minutes. A baby potato destined for smashing needs far less time than a big chunk of russet headed for mashed potatoes. Want to know more? Here’s how to get it right every time.

The essential rule for boiling potatoes: Start them in cold water. When you drop potatoes into water that’s already boiling, the outsides overcook before the centers turn tender. Starting them cold lets the potatoes and water heat up together so they cook more evenly.
points: Two keys to perfectly boiled potatoes: time and salt.
